ety: From Latin elenchus, from Ancient Greek ἔλεγχος (élenkhos, “refutation, scrutiny, control”). Doublet of elench.

ety: From cycle + -er. Piecewise doublet of wheeler.
examples: The battery cycler allows us to switch between batteries as each one runs out.

The meat of an animal slaughtered via the above method
ety: Borrowed from Punjabi ਝਟਕਾ (jhaṭkā, “sudden movement, jerking”) / جَھٹْکا (jhaṭkā). Unrelated to Slovak jatka (“slaugherhouse”) or Polish jatka (“butchershop”).

senses: A plant, Allium ursinum, a wild relative of chives and garlic.
ety: Back-formation from ramsons; compare Middle English ramson (originally plural, taken as singular); Old English hramesan, plural of hramsa (“onion, broad-leafed garlic”), from Proto-West Germanic *hramusō, from Proto-Germanic *hramusô (“onion, leek”), from Proto-Indo-European *kermus-, *kremus- (“wild garlic”). Cognate with Scots ramps (“wild garlic”), Dutch rams (“ramson”), Danish rams (“ramson”), Swedish ramslök (“wild garlic”). See buckrams.

senses: Having or furnished with doors
ety: From Middle English dored, dorryd, equivalent to door + -ed.

ety: Borrowed from Yiddish קניש (knish), from Polish knysz and Ukrainian книш (knyš).

senses: Of, concerning, or existing in both space and time.
Of or concerning spacetime.
Settled; stationary; not easily stirred or moved.
ety: From Middle English siten, seten, from Old English seten, ġeseten, past participle of sittan (“to sit”). Equivalent to sit + -en (past participle). Cognate with Dutch gezeten, German gesessen.
examples: Their fire edge might help to kindle-up old sitten-up professours.

ety: Borrowed from Thai คลอง (klɔɔng, “canal, watercourse”).
